standard.title: Australia's international interconnections
standard.description: Australia's interconnections with other countries and how these change people and places
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HS5K04 (People shape places): Students understand how people influence place characteristics. From AC9HS6K04 (Asia region diversity and location): Students have studied the Asia region's geography and location.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain Australia's interconnections with other countries, particularly in the Asia and Pacific regions, and describe how these interconnections change people and places.

nodes.label: Types of international interconnections
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the types of interconnections Australia has with other countries, including migration, trade, tourism, aid, education, defence and cultural influences.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify three types of interconnections Australia has with other countries and give one example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Describe the range of interconnections Australia has with countries in the Asia and Pacific regions: migration, trade, tourism, aid, education, defence and cultural influences — and use geospatial tools to identify geographical patterns in these connections.
wider: Investigate the volume and value of Australia's trade connections with the Asia region, and explain how these have changed over time
Examine Australia's development aid to a specific country in Asia or the Pacific, describing what the aid supports and how it affects people and places in that country
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a typology of interconnection types, students cannot distinguish between different kinds of relationships or understand how each type changes people and places in different ways. The typology is the analytical frame for all subsequent analysis.

response_modes.reason: Use a classification framework (trade / migration / aid / cultural / education / defence) and map examples to the framework before students analyse effects — this prevents conflation of different connection types.

success_criteria: Students identify at least three types of interconnections Australia has with other countries.
Students give a specific example for at least two types.

nodes.label: How interconnections change people and places
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how at least one of Australia's international interconnections changes people and places, both in Australia and in connected countries.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how one type of Australian interconnection changes people or places, with a specific example.
nodes.typical_width: Research connections between Australia and at least one country in the Asia or Pacific regions in terms of migration, trade, tourism, aid, education, defence or cultural influence, and explain the effects of at least one connection on a place in Australia and a place in another country.
wider: Investigate the effects of Australian government or non-government aid to a specific country, analysing how the aid has changed places and people's lives in that country
Examine how tourism between Australia and a specific Asian country has changed places and cultural practices in both countries, identifying both benefits and challenges

response_modes.reason: The effects of interconnections are best understood through specific case studies — choose connections with visible, concrete effects on places and communities rather than staying at the abstract level of 'trade' or 'migration'.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Australian aid to countries in Asia or the Pacific, and tourism effects, are elaboration-supported directions with concrete place-change dimensions — these are rich investigative cases with real-world data available.
success_criteria: Students explain how at least one international interconnection changes people or places.
Students give specific examples of change in both an Australian and an overseas location.

nodes.label: Geographical divisions and Australia's position
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the geographical divisions of the world including the Asia and Pacific regions, and explain Australia's position within these divisions.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the Asia and Pacific regions on a world map and describe Australia's position in relation to them.
nodes.typical_width: Use geospatial tools (globe, wall map, digital applications) to identify the geographical divisions of the world, including the Asia and Pacific regions, and explain Australia's position within the Asia-Pacific — describing how this position shapes Australia's international relationships.
wider: Use a digital mapping application to visualise Australia's connections with the Asia and Pacific regions (e.g. shipping routes, flight paths, migration flows) and explain the geographical patterns
Investigate how Australia's membership of regional bodies (e.g. APEC, ASEAN dialogue partner) reflects its geographical position and interconnections

response_modes.reason: Geographical location knowledge for the Asia-Pacific region requires spatial practice — reinforce with regular map work rather than treating location as a one-off lesson.

success_criteria: Students correctly locate the Asia and Pacific regions on a world map.
Students describe Australia's geographical position in the Asia-Pacific.

nodes.label: Evaluating interconnections and their effects
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain Australia's interconnections with other countries and evaluate how these interconnections change people and places, considering different perspectives on these effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two types of Australia's international interconnections and evaluate one positive and one negative effect on people or places.
nodes.typical_width: Explain Australia's range of international interconnections; evaluate how specific connections change people and places in Australia and in connected countries; acknowledge that different groups may experience the effects of interconnections differently.
wider: Evaluate whether Australia's interconnections with the Asia region are mutually beneficial or whether they produce unequal benefits, using evidence to support the assessment
Investigate a current issue in Australia's international relationships and assess how it illustrates the complexity of interconnections

response_modes.reason: Evaluating interconnections requires students to hold the complexity of multi-directional effects — what changes for Australia and what changes for the other country, and how these may differ. Use structured comparison to support evaluation.

success_criteria: Students explain at least two types of Australia's international interconnections.
Students evaluate the effects of at least one interconnection on both Australian and overseas places or people.
Students use relevant geographic terms (e.g. 'interconnection', 'trade', 'aid', 'migration', 'cultural influence').
